**Subject: Moving to Trunk-Based Development**

## The problem

Our long-lived feature branches routinely survive two to three weeks before merging, and every extra day multiplies the eventual merge conflict. Engineers on a twelve-person team are now stepping on each other's changes in shared modules, integration surprises surface only at merge time instead of during development, and releases slip because "finishing the merge" has become its own unplanned project. Code review quality suffers too: reviewers face 800-line diffs instead of digestible increments, so real feedback gets replaced by rubber-stamping.

## The proposal

- Adopt trunk-based development: all engineers commit small, frequent changes directly to main, gated by feature flags for anything incomplete.
- Require CI to pass (build, tests, lint) before any merge to main, with merges happening at least daily per engineer.
- Break work into tasks that can land in under a day; anything larger gets flagged and shipped dark until ready.
- Pair or mob on genuinely interdependent changes instead of branching separately and reconciling later.
- Run a two-week pilot with one squad before rolling out team-wide, so we catch process gaps before they hit everyone.

## What could go wrong

The strongest objection is real: without long-lived branches, half-finished work sits on main, and a careless flag or a mistimed toggle could expose broken functionality in production. Teams used to isolating risky work in a branch may feel trunk-based development trades a known discomfort (merge pain) for a scarier one (perpetual proximity to prod). This is a legitimate tradeoff, not a solved problem — it demands real discipline around flag hygiene, flag cleanup, and CI coverage, and it will expose any weakness in our test suite immediately rather than later.

We should also expect short-term velocity dips while the team learns to slice work smaller, and some resistance from engineers who've built workflows around branch isolation.

I would like a decision by the end of next week.
